questions.prompt: In C++23, is this function well-formed?
options: Yes: `elements_of` yields each element of any input range

questions.explanation: The yielded type of `std::generator<int>` is `int&&`. The `yield_value` overload for a general range requires the range's reference type to be convertible to the yielded type, and `int&` is not convertible to `int&&`, so overload resolution fails, the program is ill-formed, and GCC 16 rejects it. `elements_of` does accept arbitrary ranges; the fix is `elements_of(v | std::views::as_rvalue)`, or yielding `const int&` from a `std::generator<const int&>`.

In loop 2, P2718 (C++23) extends every temporary in the range-for initializer to the end of the loop, so the string outlives the iteration. Before C++23 both loops were undefined. Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: Each range-for calls `g.begin()`, and `std::generator::begin` has the precondition that the coroutine is still suspended at its initial suspend point. The first loop runs it to its final suspend point, so the second call to `begin()` violates the precondition. A generator is an input range: it cannot be restarted, and nothing in the standard makes a second pass an empty range.

questions.prompt: What does the standard say about the value of `same`?
options: It is always `true`: there is one no-op coroutine
It is always `false`

Undefined behavior: comparing no-op handles is not allowed
questions.explanation: [coroutine.noop] explicitly says that handles returned from different calls to `noop_coroutine` may or may not compare equal. Comparison itself is well-defined; only the result is left open, so code must not use equality with a fresh `noop_coroutine()` to detect the no-op handle. An implementation can return the same static frame every time, but it is not required to.

questions.prompt: What is the behavior of the second `resume()`?
options: It has no effect, because `done()` is true
Undefined behavior
It restarts the coroutine from the beginning
It calls `std::terminate`
questions.explanation: [coroutine.handle.resumption] requires that `*this` refer to a suspended coroutine that is not suspended at its final suspend point. After the first `resume()` the coroutine sits at its final suspend point, so the second call violates the precondition. A generator or task must check `done()` before resuming; the only valid operations left are `done()`, `promise()` and `destroy()`.
